name: Porter's Five Forces
use_case: A structural analysis of the competitive intensity and attractiveness of an industry by examining five forces: rivalry among existing competitors, threat of new entrants, threat of substitutes, bargaining power of suppliers, and bargaining power of buyers. Best used when assessing whether to enter a new market, launch a new product line, or evaluate the long-term defensibility of a position.
strengths: structural — surfaces forces that are easy to overlook
framework is well-known in MBA and consulting contexts
produces a defensible written analysis, not just a brainstorm
links directly to strategic posture decisions (cost leadership, differentiation, focus)
weaknesses: static snapshot — doesn't model changes over time well
originally framed for manufacturing; software/network-effect markets need adaptation
requires real industry data, not just a workshop
underweights complementors and the role of platform dynamics
use_cases: A private college is weighing a new online degree in a field where many universities, bootcamps and free courses already compete for the same students, and it wants to know how much room is left.
A logistics firm relies on two dominant software suppliers and sells to a handful of very large customers, and it wants to understand how that squeeze from both sides limits its margins.
An investor comparing two industries for an acquisition wants to know in which one established firms can keep earning healthy profits over the long run.
Our long-established product is losing sales to a cheaper offering from a different industry that meets the same need, and we want to judge how serious that threat is for the whole sector.
